articles.title: Your AI review bot is training you to ignore it
articles.description: AI code review backfires through noise. A bot that fires on style nits and speculation trains reviewers to scroll past it — exactly when it finds something real.
articles.body_html:
A year ago we turned on an AI reviewer for every PR. Last month we turned most of it off. Not because it was wrong — because it was noisy, and noise is how a review tool loses its teeth.

The decay is predictable

Week one: everyone reads every comment. Week three: the bot flags a formatting nit on line 41, a possible null on line 88, and a question about a variable name. Two of three are bikesheds. By week six, you scroll to the bottom to see if it blocked the merge, and skip the rest.

That's the trap. The bot isn't lying to you. It's just running every check it knows on every diff, and most of those checks have low precision. So the signal-to-noise ratio decays until the comments become wallpaper.

Then it catches a real one — and nobody reads it.

Precision beats recall here

For a review bot, recall is the wrong target. You don't want it to find everything; you want the things it does say to be worth stopping for. A bot that is right 80% of the time it speaks gets read. A bot that is right 40% of the time it speaks gets trained into the background.

The lever is turning down low-confidence rules. Style nits belong in the linter, not a PR comment. Speculation about intent belongs in a suggestion, not a blocking thread. The bot should be quiet by default and loud only when it has something mechanical and high-confidence.

Where the high-confidence stuff lives

The checks that survive the cull are the ones with ground truth. Not "this might be unsafe," but "the code returns 200 but the contract says 201" — a fact, checkable against a machine-readable source. Those have near-zero false positives, so when the bot speaks, it always means it.

For API changes that check is contract drift, and it's the kind of thing that's cheap to run locally and impossible for a human to eyeball. We kept that one. The variable-name comments went.

What to do this week

Open your review bot's history and count, per rule, how often a human pushed back or ignored it. The rules with the lowest strike rate get turned off first. You'll end up with a bot that comments on one in five PRs instead of every PR — and when it does, people read it.

A reviewer that nobody reads is worse than no reviewer, because it creates the feeling of coverage. How long has it been since you actually read every comment your AI reviewer left?

articles.title: Building Quidra: A Programming Language Designed for Maximum Meaning Per Token
articles.description: What if shorter code isn't always better?   I'm building Quidra, an experimental,...
articles.body_html:
What if shorter code isn't always better?

I'm building Quidra, an experimental, open-source programming language guided by one idea: Maximum Meaning Per Token (MMPT).

The goal isn't to make every program as short as possible. It's to remove unnecessary ceremony while keeping the information that helps humans, compilers, and code-generating tools understand what a program actually does.

Quidra is statically typed, implemented in C++20, and uses LLVM for native compilation. It isn't a Python wrapper or a transpiler to another high-level language.

Try it: Playground · GitHub · Website

Less syntax, but not less meaning

Consider mutation. A short function call can hide an important fact: the function might change the variable you pass to it.

In Quidra, mutable access to existing storage is explicit at both ends:

void increment(int &value)
    value += 1

int count = 7
increment(&count)

print(count)
print(NL)

The parameter int &value declares writable access. The call increment(&count) makes that authority visible to the reader without requiring them to inspect the implementation.

Yes, & is an extra token. But it conveys a distinction that can affect correctness. To me, that's a good trade.

Assignment should not secretly create aliases

Quidra uses value semantics for ordinary assignments:

int[] original = [1, 2, 3]
int[] copy = original

copy[0] = 9

Changing copy doesn't change original.

The compiler and runtime are free to optimize the implementation, including with copy-on-write, as long as observable behavior stays the same. The point is not to force expensive physical copies; it's to give assignment a predictable meaning.

Tensor shapes belong in contracts

In numerical computing, many errors come from assumptions about tensor shapes that never appear in function signatures.

Quidra can express shape constraints directly in a type:

real32 first_sample(const tensor<real32>{3, _, _} pixels)
    return pixels[0, 0, 0].item()

Here, tensor<real32>{3, _, _} means a tensor with real32 elements, exactly three dimensions, and a first dimension of size 3. The other two dimensions are unconstrained.

The const parameter also communicates that the function doesn't have permission to modify its argument.

Shape information doesn't eliminate every runtime check. But when the compiler can prove a mismatch, I'd rather find out before running the program.

Conversions should be decisions, not surprises

Quidra distinguishes mathematical numeric types from fixed-width representations. For instance, int is arbitrary-precision, while int64 and real64 have specific machine representations.

Converting an existing typed value is explicit:

int value = 10
real64 converted = real64(value)

This can be more verbose than implicit promotion. That's intentional: changing a value's representation may change its range or precision, and the source code should make that decision visible.

Quidra also supports T | error for typed failure and try for propagation, while allowing a fail-fast path when a caller doesn't need to retain the error explicitly. The aim is to make important failure contracts available without surrounding every ordinary operation with ceremony.

A native compiler, not just a syntax experiment

The Quidra compiler is written in C++20 and uses LLVM for native code generation. The project includes a REPL, JIT/AOT execution paths, diagnostics, language tooling, tensors, and automatic differentiation infrastructure.

There are also separate first-party repositories for Math, NN, Vision, Video, and DNN. Quidra is intended to be a general-purpose language, with numerical computing and machine learning as important applications—not its only use cases.

You can find the implementation, specifications, and examples in the GitHub organization.

Can language design make LLM-generated code more reliable?

This is one of the questions motivating Quidra.

LLMs can already write code in established languages. But syntax that is easy to produce isn't necessarily code that is easy to verify or safely modify.

My hypothesis is that explicit mutation, predictable value semantics, checked numeric conversions, and visible shape and error contracts could help both developers and code-generation tools reason about programs.

That is a hypothesis, not a proven advantage. Meaningful comparisons will require controlled experiments and careful attention to how much existing language knowledge an LLM has already learned.

I'm as interested in finding where this approach fails as in finding where it works.

What Quidra isn't (yet)

Quidra is experimental and pre-1.0. Its ecosystem, tooling, and real-world adoption are far smaller than those of Python, Rust, or C++. Some design decisions may change as the implementation and tests evolve.

And explicitness has a cost: sometimes a program needs more characters. MMPT is about meaningful tokens, not winning a character-count contest.

I'd love your feedback—and contributors are welcome

I'm particularly interested in these questions:

  1. Which distinctions deserve explicit syntax, and which can safely be inferred?
  2. Where would these design choices create friction in real programs?
  3. How should we measure whether a language helps people or LLMs write more reliable code?

Quidra is MIT-licensed, and I'm looking for open-source collaborators interested in compilers, C++/LLVM, language design, developer tooling, testing, documentation, math, and ML. You don't have to be a compiler expert: there are approachable first contributions, too.

  • Try Quidra in the Playground
  • Explore the source on GitHub
  • Read the contribution guide
  • Join the contributor discussion

Constructive criticism is very welcome. A language gets better when people try to break its assumptions.

Disclosure: AI assistance was used to draft and edit the English wording of this article. The design, code examples, and current implementation are documented in the linked repository.

function canStationProcessOrder(stationType, ord) {

articles.title: How to Build a Loan Amortization Schedule That Does Not Loop Forever
articles.description: A loan calculator that only prints a monthly payment is missing the part people usually need: how...
articles.body_html:
A loan calculator that only prints a monthly payment is missing the part people usually need: how much of each payment buys down principal, how much is interest, and what an extra payment changes. I built the schedule with an explicit month-by-month loop, including a guard for inputs that can never repay the balance.

The standard payment is only the starting point

The amortize function handles both ordinary interest-bearing loans and a zero-rate edge case:

function amortize(P, monthlyRate, baseN, extraPmt) {
  let payment;
  if (monthlyRate === 0) {
    payment = P / baseN;
  } else {
    const f = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, baseN);
    payment = (P * monthlyRate * f) / (f - 1);
  }
  let balance = P;
  let totalInterest = 0;
  let months = 0;
  const monthly = [];

The zero-rate branch is not optional. The usual formula divides by f - 1; when the rate is zero, that denominator is zero and the result becomes NaN. A principal divided by the number of months is the correct payment for that case.

The loop separates interest from principal

Each month calculates interest on the current balance, then applies the scheduled payment and optional extra amount:

const interest = balance * monthlyRate;
let principalPart = payment - interest + extraPmt;
if (principalPart > balance) principalPart = balance;
if (principalPart <= 0) break;
balance -= principalPart;
totalInterest += interest;
months += 1;
monthly.push({
  interest,
  principal: principalPart,
  balance: Math.max(balance, 0),
});

Clamping the last principal payment prevents the schedule from ending at a negative balance. The principalPart <= 0 check is the more important defensive detail: if a payment cannot cover interest, the balance will never shrink. Without a break, a malformed or impossible loan could make the browser hang in an infinite loop.

There is also a safety cap:

const maxMonths = baseN + 1200;
while (balance > 0.005 && months < maxMonths) {
  // ...
}

The cap is not a financial rule. It is a UI protection against pathological inputs.

Extra payments need a comparable baseline

The computed result runs the schedule once with the extra payment. If an extra amount was entered, it runs a second baseline schedule with zero extra:

if (extraPmt > 0) {
  const base = amortize(P, monthlyRate, baseN, 0);
  savedInterest = Math.max(
    base.totalInterest - totalInterest,
    0
  );
  savedMonths = Math.max(base.months - withExtra.months, 0);
}

That comparison is more useful than claiming an extra payment is “good.” It tells the user how many months and how much modeled interest the choice saves under the same principal, rate, and term.

Yearly rows are an aggregation, not a second calculation

The source walks the monthly array in groups of twelve, accumulating principalPaid, interestPaid, and the remaining balance. This keeps the chart and yearly table faithful to the exact monthly schedule. The headline total payment is P + totalInterest, not simply the advertised payment multiplied by the original term, because extra payments can shorten the schedule.

The limitations are important: rates are fixed, payments are monthly, there are no taxes, insurance, fees, refinancing, or lender-specific rounding rules. A positive extra payment is applied every month, not once. The result is a planning estimate, not a payoff quote from a bank.

Rounding and impossible loans deserve a visible policy

The internal schedule keeps fractional cents while it runs. That avoids accumulating a display-rounding error twelve times a year, but it also means the result may differ by a small amount from a lender that rounds interest on every statement. The UI formatter should be treated as presentation, not as a promise that a bank will accept the exact displayed payment.

The payment <= 0 check in the computed result is another useful boundary. A user can enter a positive principal and a negative rate, or otherwise create combinations that do not resemble a normal loan. Rather than force the loop to produce a confident-looking schedule, the view can return null when the payment cannot cover interest under the selected assumptions.

Extra payments are modeled as a monthly amount, which is a clear choice but not the only real-world choice. Some lenders apply a one-time payment immediately, some recast the payment, and some charge penalties. Those policies cannot be inferred from a generic form. The honest output is therefore “under this recurring-extra-payment model,” not “this is your official payoff date.”

If I needed lender-grade output, I would add a payment-date calendar, per-payment rounding rules, fees, and a configurable extra-payment event list. For a browser explainer, the current monthly array is a better foundation than pretending those details do not exist.

The yearly aggregation also handles a final partial year naturally. It loops until the monthly array is exhausted, so a loan paid off after 37 months produces four rows, with the last row containing only one month. That is more accurate than always multiplying a twelve-month average by four and is a nice example of why retaining the monthly schedule pays off.

Reading a schedule without confusing balance and interest

Each monthly entry carries three different ideas: the interest charged for that month, the principal removed in that month, and the balance left afterward. The yearly rows add the first two fields but carry forward the final balance. That distinction matters because cumulative interest is not the same thing as the current balance, and a chart with both lines can otherwise be surprisingly easy to misread.

The result also calculates payoff years with integer division and a remainder:

const payoffYears = Math.floor(withExtra.months / 12);
const payoffMonthsRem = withExtra.months % 12;

That presentation preserves a schedule such as 30 years and 6 months instead of rounding it to 31 years. It is a small example of keeping the internal month count authoritative while choosing a friendlier display unit afterward.

The extra-payment comparison follows the same principle. It does not pretend the extra amount changes the original contractual rate or term. It runs the same amortization logic twice, then reports the difference in months and modeled interest. If the user changes the extra payment to zero, the comparison disappears rather than showing a fabricated saving.

For testing, I would check the invariants rather than only one expected monthly payment: the balance should never become negative, each monthly principal amount should be no greater than the previous balance, and the final balance should be at or below the small stopping threshold. Those checks correspond directly to the defensive branches in the source and make regressions easier to diagnose.

I turned this amortization loop into a small free tool: Loan Amortization Calculator.
